extracted.intended_audience: booksellers, printers, engravers, publishers, librarians, and legal practitioners (18th‑century Great Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Statutory requirements governing the printing, reprinting, importation, registration, deposit, marking, and enforcement of rights in books and prints in Great Britain (18th‑century Acts). Covers consent, Stationers' register, legal deposit, penalties, time limits for actions, and rights of inventors/engravers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent required to print or reprint
rubrics_metrics.description: No person shall print, reprint, import, sell, publish, or expose to sale any book or print which is the property of a proprietor without the consent of the proprietor or proprietors first had and obtained in writing, signed in the presence of two or more credible witnesses; knowing the same to be so printed or reprinted without consent is likewise prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to obtain written consent (signed before two credible witnesses) exposes the offender to forfeiture of the offending books/prints and other penalties (see the specific forfeiture and fine provisions in the Acts). The requirement applies to both books and to engraved/etched prints as separately stated in the engraving acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationers' register entry prior to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Title to the copy of any book to be published shall, before such publication, be entered in the register book of the Company of Stationers in such manner as hath been usual; and the consent of the proprietor or proprietors must be entered in like manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each such entry requires payment of sixpence; the register book is to be kept at the Stationers' Hall and may be inspected at seasonable times by any bookseller, printer, or other person without fee. The clerk may give certificates of entry (fee not exceeding sixpence). Unless the title and consent are entered as prescribed, the forfeitures and penalties of the Act shall not be imposed on a person who prints/reprints in ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerk's refusal to register: remedy and penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the clerk of the Company of Stationers refuses or neglects to register an entry or to give a certificate when required by the author or proprietor (notice having been given by advertisement in the Gazette), then the person so refusing shall forfeit twenty pounds to the proprietor, and the proprietor shall have the like benefit as if the entry or certificate had been duly made and given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proprietor must give due notice (by Gazette advertisement) of the clerk's refusal before claiming this benefit. Penalty is recoverable in the courts of record at Westminster by action of debt, bill, plaint, or information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection and certificate of register entries
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stationers' register book may at all seasonable and convenient times be resorted to and inspected by any bookseller, printer, or other person for the purposes of ascertaining property and consent without any fee or reward; the clerk shall, when required, give a certificate under his hand of such entry or entries (fee not exceeding sixpence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspection is free; certificates are chargeable up to sixpence. Certificates serve as prima facie proof of registered title/consent and facilitate enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture and monetary penalties for unauthorized printing/selling
rubrics_metrics.description: Offenders who print, reprint, import, sell, publish, or expose to sale any book or print contrary to the Act shall forfeit such book(s) and all sheets, and shall forfeit specified sums per offending sheet/print (e.g., one penny per sheet in earlier provisions; five shillings per print in the Engraving Acts), with one moiety to the sovereign and the other to any person who shall sue for the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties vary by Act and by medium (books vs. prints) and include both destruction/forfeiture of physical copies/plates and statutory fines recoverable by specified actions in courts of record. Recovery procedures and restrictions (e.g., no wager of law, limited essoin/imparlance) are specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal deposit of copies to designated libraries (nine copies rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the specified date, nine copies of each book, upon the best paper, shall be printed and delivered by the printer to the warehouse‑keeper of the Company of Stationers at their hall before publication, for use of the Royal Library, the libraries of the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge, the four universities in Scotland, the Library of Sion College in London, and the Faculty of Advocates at Edinburgh respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The warehouse‑keeper is required, within ten days after demand by keepers of the respective libraries or authorized persons, to deliver the copies for their use. Failure to deliver incurs forfeiture of £5 for every copy not delivered plus the value of the copy; recovery may be by the Queen's Majesty and the specified institutions with full costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty for failing to deliver deposited copies
rubrics_metrics.description: If proprietor, bookseller, printer, or the warehouse‑keeper fails to deliver the required printed copies as directed by the Act, they shall forfeit, besides the value of the printed copies, the sum of five pounds for every copy not so delivered; the value of the copies is also recoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery may be pursued by the sovereign and the named libraries/universities/colleges with full costs. The statute fixes strict monetary penalties in addition to the value of the missing copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for foreign‑language imports
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the Act shall be construed to prohibit the importation, vending, or selling of any books in Greek, Latin, or any other language printed beyond the seas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This carve‑out preserves trade in certain foreign‑language imports despite broader restrictions on printing/reprinting within the kingdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of importation of books reprinted abroad (12 Geo. II c.36)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the specified date it is declared unlawful to import into the kingdom for sale any book first composed or written and printed and published in this kingdom and reprinted abroad; importation for sale of such reprints is prohibited and offenders shall forfeit the books and incur fines (five pounds and double the value of each book), with one moiety to the King and the other to the informer/plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Act contains exceptions (e.g., not to extend to any book that has not been printed or reprinted in this kingdom within twenty years before importation). Penalties are recoverable in the Courts of Record at Westminster or, for Scotland, before the Court of Session by summary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price‑setting complaints and judicial/regulatory price limitation (repealed clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any bookseller or printer sets a price conceived by others to be too high or unreasonable, any person may complain to named high officers and judges (Archbishop of Canterbury, Lord Chancellor, Chief Justices, Vice‑Chancellors, etc.), who may summon the bookseller, enquire into the price, and reform, redress, limit and settle the price deemed just and reasonable; sale afterwards at a higher rate incurs a forfeiture of five pounds per book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clause provides a procedure for complaint, enquiry, and written settlement (with public notice by Gazette); costs of complaint may be awarded against the bookseller when rate is altered. Note: the text records this clause was subsequently repealed by later statute (15 Geo. II c. 3d), so applicability depends on temporal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits for bringing actions for offences (limitation periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions, suits, bills, indictments, or informations for offences against the Act must be brought within three months next after such offence committed (or, in some provisions, within three months after discovery of the offence); in the Engraving Acts a prosecution must be commenced within six calendar months after the offence committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different Acts set different limitation periods (three months generally for book offences; three months after discovery in some clauses; six months for engraving-related prosecutions). Failure to commence within the prescribed period renders the action void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural defense and costs on unsuccessful plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: In actions brought under these Acts the defendant may plead the general issue and give special matter in evidence; if verdict is for defendant or plaintiff becomes nonsuited or discontinues, the defendant shall have and recover full costs as in other cases by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grants typical procedural defenses and cost recovery to defendants in enforcement actions under the statutes; defendants receive the same remedies as in ordinary civil litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights vested in inventors/engravers of prints (term and form requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who invent, design, engrave, etch, or work in mezzotinto or chiaro oscuro (or from their own works) any historical or other print shall have the sole right and liberty of printing and reprinting the same for the term of fourteen years from the first publishing; plates shall be truly engraved with the name of the proprietor on each plate and printed on every such print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement (engraving, copying, selling, importing copies without proprietor's consent) triggers forfeiture of plates and sheets and monetary penalties (e.g., five shillings per infringing print). Later statutes extended protection to prints taken from pictures, drawings, models, sculptures, and to portraits, landscapes, architecture, maps, charts, etc., and provided enforcement/remedies analogous to book provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser of plates entitled to print without penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall be lawful for any person who purchases any plate or plates from the original proprietors to print and reprint the plates without incurring any of the penalties mentioned in the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act distinguishes the rights of the original proprietor from rights that attach to a bona fide purchaser of the physical plate; sale of the plate transfers the practical ability to print without penalty from the vendor under this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public act and judicial notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act shall be deemed and taken to be a public act and be judicially taken notice of as such by all Judges, Justices, and other persons whatsoever, without specially pleading the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision obviates the need to specially plead the statute in court; courts take official notice of the Act as public law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoveries, distribution of penalties, and procedural restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties are generally recoverable by action of debt, bill, plaint, or information in the Courts of Record at Westminster (or Court of Session for Scotland); one moiety of penalties goes to the sovereign (King/Queen) and the other to any person(s) who shall sue for the same; in actions certain procedural protections/restrictions are specified (no wager of law, limited essoin, privilege, or more than one imparlance allowed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Acts prescribe both the venue and the manner of recovery and allocate the fiscal proceeds of penalties to the Crown and to private enforcers, encouraging private suits (common informers) subject to procedural constraints.
